source.title: Training-free Truthfulness Detection via Value Vectors in LLMs
source.authors: Runheng Liu; Heyan Huang; Xing-Chen Xiao; Zhi-Jing Wu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies truthfulness-related signals in MLP value vectors, but does not test superposition, feature-capacity competition, SAE feature recovery, or the geometry of overlapping features.
record.gate_note: The paper reports sparse truthfulness-related signals in individual MLP value vectors, which are relevant to the broader subject but do not measure any listed claim version. TruthV benchmark scores measure a detection method's performance, not superposition, and are not included as claim-result rows. Hyperparameter values used to select vectors are also omitted.
record.test_reason: The study ranks individual MLP value vectors (neurons) by how well their activations pick the correct multiple-choice answer, then builds a truthfulness detector (TruthV) from them. It never measures feature overlap, capacity competition, sparsity transitions, polysemanticity, SAE recovery or feature dimensionality. It does not mention superposition at all, so 'discusses' overstates the link. The closest enum value for an unrelated study is used.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: a sparse subset of MLP value vectors shows systematic, directionally consistent activation differences between truthful and untruthful content. This supports a training-free detector (TruthV) that beats NoVo and log-likelihood baselines across benchmarks and model scales from 2B to 13B.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or adapt the original toy-model superposition method; it measures MLP value-vector activation correlations for truthfulness detection.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that selected-vector performance varies with ensemble size and that the optimal selection fraction varies across LLMs; it also reports that pooled activation distributions overlap despite consistent within-question ordering.

fits_no_version.finding: A sparse subset of individual MLP value vectors (selected at about 0.1% in the ensemble) predicts answer correctness well above chance, while most vectors are near chance. The signal is relative within each question rather than an absolute threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In instruction-tuned LLMs, truthfulness-predictive signal is concentrated in a sparse set of individual MLP neurons in middle and late layers and expressed as within-context relative activation.

fits_no_version.finding: Top truthfulness vectors projected to the vocabulary show no surface-level semantic alignment, and t-SNE shows no clustering. The authors speculate the vectors encode abstract or distributed properties; this is untested.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual neurons predictive of an abstract property such as truthfulness need not be interpretable through vocabulary projection.

record.problems: The paper does not directly test any listed superposition claim. Main benchmark tables do not report error bars or confidence intervals; the explicit 10-run mean-accuracy protocol applies to the AdvGLUE and HaluEval evaluations. The PIQA activation-distribution analysis selects the vector on the training set and examines it on the same data.
record.rows_left_out: TruthV benchmark accuracy tables and ablations were left out because they report the detection method's performance rather than a result about feature superposition or geometry. Figure-only vector-accuracy and layer-distribution values were recorded only through the paper's verbal descriptions.

untested.parts: All: toy networks, sparsity-dependent transition, near-orthogonal overlapping directions, geometry.
All: capacity competition and dedicated versus shared dimensions.
All: distribution of features across neurons and SAE recovery. Truthfulness signal is located in individual neurons, with no test of distributed or superposed coding.
All: dimensionality of features is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: No superposition-related result. The detector benchmark tables and ablations (Tables 1–6, 10, 11) are rightly excluded as method-performance results. The noun-masking ablation (Table 11) bears only on whether the signal depends on content, not on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity-dependent transitions, overlap, near-orthogonality, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Feature distribution across neurons and recovery of sparse features with a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of representation.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-Chat, Gemma-2-2B-it, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Qwen3-4B (aggregate verbal finding)
rows.size_stated: 2B to 7B models; individual sizes are given in the model names
rows.operation_detail: Ranked individual MLP value vectors by accuracy in predicting correct answers from final-token activations.

conditions.value: multiple-choice datasets; examples shown include QASC, SWAG, HSwag, and SIQA
at least 1000 per vector's accuracy computation

rows.measure: Per-vector answer-choice accuracy relative to random guessing
rows.value: The authors state that most value vectors perform close to chance, while a small subset performs substantially above chance; some vectors fall below chance under argmax and improve under argmin.
rows.note: The paper gives a QASC random-prediction probability example, but no exact accuracy values for the plotted vector results in the text. This is evidence of sparse truthfulness-predictive signals, not a test of feature superposition.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The state describes the authors' own finding (a sparse subset of vectors well above chance, most near chance), not any claim version.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-Chat, Gemma-2-2B-it, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Qwen3-4B (aggregate verbal finding)
rows.size_stated: 2B to 7B models; individual sizes are given in the model names
rows.operation_detail: Examined the layer distribution of the top 0.01% of value vectors by accuracy.
rows.measure: Layer-wise distribution of selected value vectors
rows.value: The authors state that these vectors are predominantly in the middle and final layers, with none in the early layers.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Layer-wise distribution of truthfulness-related value vectors; Figure 3
rows.note: This is a distribution across model layers, not a measurement of geometric overlap or feature dimensionality.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The selection threshold is inconsistent in the paper: the text says top 0.1%, the Figure 3 caption says top 0.01%. The row gives only 0.01% and should note the discrepancy.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-Chat, Gemma-2-2B-it, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Qwen3-4B (aggregate verbal finding)
rows.size_stated: 2B to 7B models; individual sizes are given in the model names
rows.operation_detail: Compared truthful and untruthful answer activations for the highest-accuracy value vector on PIQA.

conditions.value: highest-accuracy value vector selected on the training set

rows.measure: Distributions of key activation magnitudes for truthful and untruthful inputs
rows.value: The pooled distributions overlap substantially across models, while the truthful answer's activation is consistently higher or lower than its untruthful alternative within each question, depending on the activation pattern.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Context-dependent key activations of truthfulness-related value vectors; Figure 4
rows.note: The authors attribute pooled overlap to question-specific activation ranges. This concerns context-dependent activation comparisons, not overlap between represented feature directions.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The vector is selected on the PIQA training set and examined on the same data, so the within-question ordering claim is in-sample. It is also a verbal claim with no reported per-question statistic.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
